for all of the problems considered, the computational complexity is NP-hard, but we are able to provide polynomial-time exact and/or approximation algorithms for a variety of biologically relevant special cases of the problem.
the problem is hard to solve exactly in the general case and hard to approximate within a factor less than 1.5 in general, but can be solved efficiently in many biologically interesting cases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, if the forbidden rooted triplets are few, then we can find an optimal solution efficiently; otherwise, if the number of the allowed rooted triplets is small, then we can still find an optimal solution in a reasonable time.
the more we can specify the evolutionary history of the species, the easier the problem becomes.
we provide efficient exact and approximation solutions for a number of variants of the problem, which are all NP-hard.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to efficiently infer a phylogenetically meaningful tree/network even when the set of forbidden triplets is quite large.
the presence of a small number of rooted triplets in F can be used to rule out a large number of trees as possible solutions.

, in many practical scenarios, it is possible to efficiently compute a phylogenetic network that is consistent with a given set of rooted triplets and that is free from a given set of forbidden rooted triplets.
